concepts.gloss: A restricted overlap whereby condition or reason phrases can qualify a situation, proposition or speech act.
Discourse prominence or primary stress on an element, distinct from the scopal focus of adverbs such as only.
Whether a constituent can be informationally focused in an interrogative, negation contrast or cleft.
A dependent that affects the truth conditions of the proposition, as a temporal modifier can.
An evaluative dependent not altering whether the described situation occurred.
The capacity of an adjunct class to be targeted by an interrogative expression such as when or why.
The semantic scope of one adjunct relative to another or to negation.
The capacity of a goal or extent to make a clause describe a bounded event.
A situation presented with a terminal boundary, such as an accomplishment with a goal.
An activity presented without a terminal endpoint.
The surface category forming an adjunct, including AdvP, PP, NP, or finite, non-finite and verbless clauses.

concepts.term: front, central and end adjunct positions
concepts.gloss: The three coarse linear positions of adjuncts, with multiple adjuncts possible in front or end.
A dependent concerning a speaker's communicative act rather than merely the event described.
An adjunct qualifying the status or likelihood of a proposition.
An adjunct conveying a speaker evaluation of a situation, typically non-restrictive.

rules.concept: ordinary, modal and speech act-related uses of condition and reason adjuncts
rules.statement: Conditional adjuncts may have basic, modal, or speech act-related readings, while reason adjuncts may express an ordinary reason or a reason for the speaker's assertion.
rules.condition: For an if-headed conditional, distinguish a condition on the situation, a qualification of the proposition, and a comment on the speech act. For a because-headed reason adjunct, distinguish a cause or reason for the situation from grounds offered for the speaker's assertion.

contrast.text: We will train outside if the weather is dry. [ordinary conditional]
If I remember correctly, the team trains on Saturday. [modal qualification]
The team trains on Saturday, if you were wondering. [speech act-related conditional]
Leah stayed home because it was icy. [reason for action]
Leah must be home, because her bicycle is outside. [reason for asserting a conclusion]

rules.statement: Integrated temporal-location adjuncts can typically be informational focus in alternative questions, contrastive negation and clefts, whereas evaluative supplements such as fortunately resist such focus.
rules.condition: Compare integrated temporal-location modifiers with evaluative supplements in alternative questions, contrastive negation and it-clefts, allowing that the cleft construction has a narrower range of focal elements.

exceptions.description: It-clefts permit a narrower set of focus elements than alternative questions and contrastive negation; some -ly adverbs are less readily focused in clefts.

contrast.text: The singer arrived on Thursday. [temporal adjunct]
Was it on Thursday that the singer arrived? [cleft focus]
Fortunately, the singer arrived safely. [evaluative supplement]
?Was it fortunately that the singer arrived safely? [evaluative adjunct resists focus]
Did the boat move quickly or slowly? [alternative question]
?Was it quickly that the boat moved? [cleft with -ly adverb is less natural]

rules.review_notes: The source distinguishes informational from scopal focus; this is not an absolute prohibition for all adjuncts. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed.

rules.statement: Restrictive adjuncts affect the assertion's truth conditions; non-restrictive evaluative adjuncts do not, while a modal adjunct can be truth-relevant despite resisting focus.
rules.condition: Compare a temporal-location modifier, evaluative supplement and epistemic modal adjunct by whether the adjunct contributes to what would make the described proposition true.

contrast.text: The parcel arrived yesterday. [restrictive temporal qualification]
Fortunately, the parcel arrived. [non-restrictive evaluation]
The parcel probably arrived. [truth-relevant modal qualification; arrival not entailed]
Surprisingly, the committee agreed. [non-restrictive evaluation]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source/index was provided; no comparative analysis is inferred.

rules.review_notes: Lack of focus does not entail non-restrictiveness. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed.

rules.statement: Most adjunct categories can be questioned by a suitable wh-phrase, but evaluative adjuncts cannot; both reason and purpose can be questioned by why.
rules.condition: When selecting an interrogative to target a clause adjunct, check its semantic type: temporal location can use when, reason and purpose can both use why, whereas speaker evaluation has no corresponding adjunct wh-question.

contrast.text: When did Noor arrive? — On Monday. [temporal location]
Why did Noor open the gate? — To allow the guests in. [purpose]
Why did Noor leave? — Because she felt unwell. [reason]
Fortunately, Noor reached the station. [evaluation is not a questionably targeted adjunct]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source/index was provided; no comparative analysis is inferred.

rules.review_notes: Most, not all, adjunct categories are question-compatible. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed.

rules.concept: scope of evaluative and modal adjuncts over frequency
rules.statement: Evaluative and epistemic modal adjuncts can take wider semantic scope than frequency adjuncts within the same clause.
rules.condition: When an evaluative or epistemic modal adjunct co-occurs with a frequency adjunct, distinguish the reading in which the evaluation or modality applies to the whole frequency-qualified proposition.

contrast.text: Fortunately, Iris seldom misses the train. [evaluation over seldom]
Iris probably visits the library regularly. [probably over regularly]
Happily, the team usually finishes early. [evaluation over usually]

rules.concept: bounding effects of goal and extent dependents
rules.statement: A terminal goal or extent can turn an unbounded activity reading into a bounded accomplishment reading, affecting how in- and for-duration expressions combine with the clause.
rules.condition: Compare an atelic activity lacking a terminal goal with a counterpart whose goal PP or extent NP specifies an endpoint; the latter can support a bounded reading expressed with in-duration.

contrast.text: Omar jogged for fifteen minutes. [unbounded activity]
Omar jogged to the harbour in fifteen minutes. [bounded goal]
Omar walked three kilometres in forty minutes. [measured extent]
Omar jogged along the path for fifteen minutes. [nonterminal path]

rules.statement: Adjuncts are most often AdvPs or PPs but can also be NPs, finite or non-finite clauses, or verbless clauses, with form and semantic function distinguished.
rules.condition: When classifying the form of an adjunct, analyse its constituent as AdvP, PP, NP, inverted conditional finite clause, infinitival, gerund-participial, past-participial or verbless clause as licensed, rather than equating its semantic function with a syntactic category.

contrast.text: Jules responded quietly. [AdvP]
Jules responded after the inspection. [PP]
Jules arrived last Wednesday. [NP]
Had Jules received the notice, she would have replied. [finite conditional]
Jules stayed late to complete the repair. [infinitival purpose]
Noticing the smoke, Jules opened the window. [gerund-participial]
The curtains drawn, Mira switched on the lamp. [past-participial adjunct]
His hands in his pockets, Milo entered the room. [verbless adjunct]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source/index was provided; no comparative analysis is inferred.

rules.review_notes: With non-finite and verbless clauses the precise semantic relation is often pragmatically inferred. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed.

rules.concept: front central and end positions of adjuncts
rules.statement: The coarse placement distinction for clause adjuncts is front, central, and end; more than one adjunct may appear at the front or end.
rules.condition: When describing a clause adjunct's linear position, choose front, central or end relative to the clause structure, allowing multiple front or end adjuncts; finer central-position contrasts are treated elsewhere.

contrast.text: Fortunately, there was enough time. [front]
There was fortunately enough time. [central]
There was enough time, fortunately. [end]
Yesterday beside the river, we found a lost glove. [two front adjuncts]
We camped on the hillside for three nights. [two end adjuncts]
